title: From US Software Job to Rs 36 Lakh Moringa Farm in Maharashtra
excerpt: Sagar Khare walked away from a high-paying American tech job, returned to his village in Solapur, and built a profitable organic moringa business on five acres.
body:
• Sagar Khare, a software engineer, left a high-paying job in the United States and returned to his village of Kurduwadi in Maharashtra's Solapur district to farm full-time.
  • He now grows organic moringa (drumstick) on five acres of land, earning an annual income of about Rs 36 lakh.
  • He first rebuilt his soil's health and researched heat-tolerant crops suited to Solapur's 45°C summers, visiting moringa farmers in Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh before planting.
  • His story, spotlighted by the Instagram page Founders Vision, has become a reference point for diaspora professionals weighing a return to agriculture.

From Code to Cultivation

Sagar Khare had what many aspire to: a high-paying software engineering job in the United States. He gave it up. Khare returned to Kurduwadi, his village in Maharashtra's Solapur district, where his parents practised traditional farming, and chose to work the land full-time, according to NDTV, which cited reporting by The Economic Times.

Growing up around agriculture had left its mark. "My work was good, but I enjoyed being on the farm more," Khare said. That preference, discovered in childhood and confirmed across an ocean, became the basis of a career change few in his position attempt.

Why Moringa

Khare did not plant at random. He turned to organic moringa farming after noticing the rising costs and impact of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, and he began by improving the health of his soil before sowing a single crop. Solapur's climate shaped the choice: summers there can push past 45°C, so he researched crops that could withstand the heat and still fetch a strong price.

That research led him to moringa, the drumstick tree prized for its leaves and pods. Before committing his five acres, Khare visited farmers in Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh to understand the crop and its commercial potential firsthand. The diligence paid off: he now earns about Rs 36 lakh annually from organic moringa.

A Template for Returning NRIs

Khare's story, amplified by a post from the Instagram page Founders Vision, resonates with a growing audience of diaspora professionals who fantasize about leaving corporate life for something of their own. Entrepreneurship carries real risk, and Khare's own path required patience, agronomy and capital discipline. But his experience also reframes what modern farming looks like in India: less about brute labor, more about crop selection, soil science and market awareness.

The lesson he embodies is one the diaspora keeps rediscovering. While many chase city jobs and foreign salaries, wealth can grow directly from land already owned — provided it is worked with knowledge rather than nostalgia. For Khare, the answer to a high-paying American career was, as the saying in his village might go, right there all along: five acres in Kurduwadi, planted with moringa.
